options: Enshrined abortion rights in the state constitution
quiz.explanation: Arizona voters enshrined abortion rights in the state constitution, superseding the revived 1864 near-total ban.

laws.title: Water Crisis and Colorado River Compact Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Arizona Faces Mandatory Water Cuts from Lake Mead Shortage
laws.fullDescription: Arizona continued facing severe Colorado River water cuts as Lake Mead remained at historically low levels. The state negotiated its share of mandatory reductions under the Drought Contingency Plan and the 2026 post-2026 operating guidelines. Agricultural water users bore most cuts while urban areas prioritized conservation and recycled water.
laws.penalty: Federal Bureau of Reclamation water delivery reductions; compact compliance requirements
exceptions: Tribal water rights protected
Groundwater alternatives development allowed

quiz.q: What body of water determines Arizona's mandatory Colorado River cuts?
quiz.explanation: Lake Mead levels determine mandatory Colorado River water cuts under the Drought Contingency Plan, with Arizona taking significant reductions as the reservoir fell.

laws.title: Maricopa County Election Disputes and Certification
laws.subtitle: Arizona Courts Uphold Election Results Repeatedly
laws.fullDescription: Arizona continued to be a battleground for election disputes, with the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors facing pressure not to certify results. Courts consistently upheld certifications and rejected election denial claims. Arizona's election procedures became among the most scrutinized in the nation.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for interfering with election certification
exceptions: Legal challenge rights maintained
Recount provisions

quiz.q: How have Arizona courts handled repeated election denial challenges?
options: Consistently upheld certifications and rejected claims
quiz.explanation: Arizona courts consistently upheld election certifications and rejected election denial claims, while Maricopa County continued facing pressure from election deniers.

laws.title: Election Law Changes and Voting Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Arizona Enacts New Voter Registration Requirements
laws.fullDescription: Arizona enacted new laws requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration in federal elections, following up on state-level proof requirements. Federal courts debated the constitutionality while states and federal government clashed over voter registration standards. Arizona became a focal point for voting rights litigation.
laws.penalty: Rejection of registrations without proof; criminal penalties for fraud
exceptions: Motor voter automatic registration challenged
Military and overseas voter provisions

quiz.q: What new voter registration requirement did Arizona implement for federal elections?
quiz.explanation: Arizona required documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration in federal elections, a controversial measure that faced constitutional challenges.

laws.title: TSMC Phoenix Fab and Semiconductor Jobs
laws.subtitle: Arizona Attracts Trillion-Dollar Chip Industry
laws.fullDescription: Arizona attracted the first US TSMC semiconductor fab in Phoenix with $6.6 billion in federal CHIPS Act funding, adding thousands of high-wage semiconductor manufacturing jobs. Intel also expanded its Arizona fab operations. The state positioned itself as a semiconductor manufacturing hub alongside Texas and Ohio.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; federal subsidy compliance requirements
exceptions: CHIPS Act domestic content requirements
National security review for foreign workers

quiz.q: Besides TSMC, what other major chip company has major fab operations in Arizona?
quiz.explanation: Intel has major semiconductor fabrication operations in Chandler, Arizona, making Arizona a two-way semiconductor manufacturing hub alongside the TSMC Phoenix fab.

laws.title: Groundwater Depletion and Suburban Development Halt
laws.subtitle: Arizona forces developers to prove water supply before building
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's rapid growth in suburbs like Rio Verde and parts of Scottsdale has exposed a fundamental problem: insufficient water. The state's Department of Water Resources denied water adequacy designations for parts of the Phoenix metro, effectively halting new housing development. Underground aquifer levels are dropping dramatically in some areas. The state passed new groundwater management legislation strengthening requirements. The conflict between growth ambitions and water reality is reshaping Arizona's development patterns.
laws.penalty: Developers cannot build subdivisions without demonstrating 100-year water supply adequacy
exceptions: In-fill development in established served areas exempt from new adequacy requirements
Agricultural land conversions to residential must include water supply analysis

laws.title: Data Center Desert Boom and Water Consumption
laws.subtitle: Arizona attracts data centers but faces water conflict from cooling needs
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has attracted massive data center investment — Meta, Microsoft, Google, and others have huge campuses in the Phoenix metro. But data centers use enormous amounts of water for cooling in a desert with severe water scarcity. Arizona is examining water usage for data centers as the Colorado River crisis intensifies. Some municipalities are restricting new data center water use. The tension between tech economic development and water sustainability is acute in the Sonoran Desert.
laws.penalty: New data center developments must demonstrate water supply adequacy in stressed basins
exceptions: Air-cooled and liquid-cooled systems without evaporative cooling have lighter water requirements
Data centers in less-stressed groundwater basins have different regulatory treatment

laws.title: Swing State Status and Election Administration Battles
laws.subtitle: Arizona's close elections trigger audit controversies and voting law battles
laws.fullDescription: Arizona became a national battleground after Biden's narrow 2020 victory and the subsequent 'Cyber Ninjas' audit ordered by Republicans that confirmed Biden's win. Arizona has been ground zero for both voting restriction legislation and voting access expansion battles. Maricopa County, with 4 million residents, is the second-largest voting jurisdiction in the US. Arizona's competitive status — flipping purple after decades as reliably Republican — makes it a constant focus of national political attention.
laws.penalty: Election fraud carries criminal penalties; systematic fraud schemes face federal prosecution
exceptions: Provisional ballots for voters with address discrepancies must be counted after verification
Mail voting is a right in Arizona; requests cannot be denied without cause

quiz.q: What did Arizona's 'Cyber Ninjas' audit find?
options: Biden won by more votes than originally certified
Biden's 2020 victory confirmed even by Republican-ordered audit
Systematic ballot tampering requiring new election
quiz.explanation: The Cyber Ninjas audit — ordered by Arizona Republicans hoping to overturn the 2020 election — confirmed Biden's victory, finding Biden actually won by a slightly larger margin than originally certified.

laws.title: Groundwater Depletion and Phoenix Growth Limits
laws.subtitle: Arizona confronting aquifer exhaustion in the desert Southwest
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's explosive population growth in Phoenix, Tucson, and surrounding areas has occurred in one of the world's most water-stressed regions. The state depends on three water sources: Colorado River allocations, Salt River Project water, and groundwater. After Arizona faced potential Colorado River cuts due to drought and overallocation, the state has invested in water security — including recharging aquifers and securing alternative supplies. However, rural Arizona communities outside regulated areas face acute groundwater depletion from both agricultural use and residential development. Rio Verde Highlands, a Phoenix suburb, made national news when the city cut off water deliveries it had provided informally, forcing residents who had built homes without secured water supply to face crisis. Arizona's Groundwater Management Act (1980) was pioneering but left significant gaps. New subdivisions in some areas were approved without verified 100-year water supply, creating long-term liability.
laws.penalty: Water rights violations carry civil and criminal penalties; unauthorized wells face closure orders
exceptions: Grandfathered irrigation rights predate the 1980 Groundwater Management Act

quiz.q: What water crisis made Rio Verde Highlands, a Phoenix suburb, nationally famous?
options: A contamination event from industrial pollution
Phoenix cut off informal water deliveries, leaving residents without water supply
A dam failure that flooded the community
Discovery that the community's wells were contaminated with arsenic
quiz.explanation: Rio Verde Highlands made national news when Phoenix cut off water deliveries it had informally provided to the suburb, leaving residents who had built homes without a secured water supply facing a severe crisis in the Arizona desert.

laws.title: Semiconductor Manufacturing Investment and TSMC Arizona
laws.subtitle: Arizona becoming America's chip manufacturing hub
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has attracted the most significant semiconductor manufacturing investment in the United States, centered on TSMC's decision to build fabs in Phoenix — the first time TSMC has manufactured chips outside of Taiwan. The first fab, producing 4nm chips, began production in 2024. Intel has also expanded significantly at its Chandler campus, and a cluster of supporting chip equipment and materials companies has developed. The CHIPS Act provided billions in subsidies for these investments. Arizona offers semiconductor manufacturers a combination of land availability, relatively stable geology, sunshine (for solar power), and proximity to academic institutions (ASU and University of Arizona). The chip industry brings high-paying jobs but also significant water consumption in one of the nation's most water-stressed states. The Arizona-Taiwan tech relationship has deepened through TSMC's investment.
laws.penalty: Semiconductor manufacturing facilities must comply with environmental regulations including water use permits and hazardous material handling requirements
exceptions: CHIPS Act funding comes with domestic content and national security provisions for facilities receiving subsidies

quiz.q: Why is TSMC's Arizona facility historically significant?
options: It is TSMC's largest facility in the world
It is the first time TSMC has manufactured chips outside of Taiwan
It produces the world's most advanced 2nm chips
It is the first fully automated chip manufacturing facility
quiz.explanation: TSMC's Arizona fabs are the first time TSMC has manufactured chips outside of Taiwan — a historically significant diversification driven by geopolitical concerns about Taiwan's vulnerability and US CHIPS Act incentives.

laws.title: Election Integrity Battles and Voting Restriction Laws
laws.subtitle: Arizona at the center of American democracy debates
laws.fullDescription: Arizona became a central battleground in debates over US election integrity following the 2020 presidential election, which Joe Biden narrowly won in the state. The Republican-led legislature commissioned a private audit (the Cyber Ninjas audit) of Maricopa County ballots — the most extensive election audit in US history — which ultimately confirmed Biden's victory but raised questions about the process. Arizona has subsequently passed multiple voting restriction laws including stricter proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration, shorter deadlines for mail ballot requests, and stricter signature matching. Courts have blocked some of these laws while others have been implemented. Arizona's experience has become a template for election law debates nationally, with both parties investing heavily in Arizona election infrastructure and litigation.
laws.penalty: Election fraud carries criminal penalties; improper voting registration can result in prosecution
exceptions: Federal law protects some voting rights that state restrictions cannot override, including for overseas and military voters

quiz.q: What was the Cyber Ninjas audit in Arizona?
options: A cybersecurity review of Arizona's election systems
A private audit of Maricopa County ballots commissioned by the Republican legislature after 2020
A federal investigation into election fraud claims
An independent audit of voter registration databases
quiz.explanation: The Cyber Ninjas audit was a private audit of Maricopa County, Arizona ballots commissioned by the Republican-led state legislature after the 2020 election — the most extensive election audit in US history, which ultimately confirmed Biden's victory.

laws.title: Colorado River Compact Renegotiation
laws.subtitle: Seven states fight over shrinking water amid megadrought
laws.fullDescription: Arizona and six other states that draw water from the Colorado River faced a crisis as Lake Mead and Lake Powell fell to historic lows. The federal government imposed mandatory water cuts on lower basin states for the first time. Arizona, Nevada and California agreed to voluntary conservation deals funded by federal Inflation Reduction Act money. The century-old Colorado River Compact, written when the river ran higher than it does today, requires renegotiation for 2026. The river simply cannot support all claimed rights.
laws.penalty: Water allocation cuts mandatory for states that fail to conserve; senior water rights holders protected before junior rights
exceptions: Tribal water rights have complex legal standing and some protections
Agricultural users hold senior rights in most western water law systems

quiz.q: When was the original Colorado River Compact written that requires renegotiation?
quiz.explanation: The Colorado River Compact was written in the 1920s (1922) when the river appeared to run higher than it actually does on average, and all seven states' water claims exceed the river's actual sustainable supply—requiring renegotiation for 2026.

laws.title: Waymo Robotaxi Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: Arizona pioneers autonomous vehicle commercial deployment
laws.fullDescription: Arizona established itself as the leading state for autonomous vehicle testing and deployment, with Waymo launching fully commercial driverless rides in Phoenix without safety drivers. Arizona's permissive regulatory environment—no special permits required for AV testing—attracted most major AV companies. Waymo has expanded to other cities but Phoenix remains its most mature commercial deployment. Questions about liability, insurance and traffic law compliance for autonomous vehicles are gradually being addressed by state law and court decisions.
laws.penalty: Autonomous vehicles must comply with all existing traffic laws; liability for accidents assigned to operators under current frameworks
exceptions: AV companies may operate under alternative compliance frameworks for novel situations
Data from AVs protected as proprietary with some public safety exceptions

quiz.q: Which company has deployed the most commercially mature driverless car service in Phoenix, Arizona?
quiz.explanation: Waymo (Google's AV subsidiary) has the most commercially mature driverless car service in Phoenix, Arizona, operating fully commercial rides without safety drivers—the most advanced commercial deployment of autonomous vehicles globally.

laws.title: Water Wars and Sun Belt Growth Limits
laws.subtitle: Arizona's explosive growth hits fundamental water constraint
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has been one of America's fastest-growing states for decades, but growth is increasingly constrained by water availability. The Rio Verde Highlands community lost its water supply when the City of Scottsdale cut off deliveries in 2023. New housing developments require developers to prove 100-year water supply. The state's major water source—the Colorado River—is over-allocated and declining. Arizona's paradox of being a desert state with explosive population growth is reaching a reckoning.
laws.penalty: 100-year adequate water supply certification required for new residential development; water rights transfers regulated
exceptions: Existing developments with grandfathered water rights continue
Agricultural water rights can be fallowed and leased to municipal users

quiz.q: What did Arizona require developers to prove before approving new housing developments?
quiz.explanation: Arizona requires developers to prove a 100-year adequate water supply before new residential developments can be approved—a law that is increasingly challenging to satisfy as the Colorado River declines and the state's fast growth continues.

laws.title: Arizona Renewable Energy Standard
laws.subtitle: Solar Power in the Sunniest State
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Renewable Energy Standard and Tariff (REST) requires utilities to obtain 15% of retail electricity sales from renewable sources by 2025, with at least 30% of that from distributed resources like rooftop solar. Arizona, with over 300 sunny days a year, has become a major solar state — both utility-scale and residential. However, Arizona has been criticized for not having a stronger standard, and conflicts between the utility APS and rooftop solar customers over net metering rates have been contentious.
laws.penalty: Utilities failing to meet RES must pay alternative compliance fees per kWh shortfall
exceptions: Cooperative utilities under separate regulations
Municipal utilities may adopt equivalent standards

laws.title: Arizona Heat Emergency Protocols
laws.subtitle: Extreme Heat as Public Health Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Arizona, particularly the Phoenix metropolitan area, faces the deadliest heat in the US — over 400 heat-related deaths occur annually in Maricopa County alone, making it the county with the most heat deaths in the nation. Arizona law requires the Arizona Department of Health Services to coordinate a statewide heat response, and Maricopa County has pioneered 'cooling center' networks, heat watch systems, and medical examiner heat death certification. As climate change intensifies Phoenix's heat island, public health law must evolve to address extreme heat as a leading environmental killer.
laws.penalty: Heat safety violations in workplaces: OSHA penalties; employers liable for worker heat illness without adequate precautions
exceptions: Outdoor work with documented heat illness prevention programs
Emergency response workers

laws.title: Arizona Proposition 206 — Minimum Wage and Paid Sick Time
laws.subtitle: Voters Override the Legislature
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters approved Proposition 206 in 2016, setting a path to $12/hour minimum wage and requiring all employers to provide earned paid sick time — up to 40 hours for small employers and 40 hours for large employers. This was significant because the Arizona legislature had previously preempted local minimum wage increases by Phoenix and Flagstaff. The initiative bypassed the legislature entirely. Arizona's minimum wage has continued increasing with inflation, reaching $14.35/hour in 2024. Paid sick time was expanded under subsequent legislation to cover COVID-related leave.
laws.penalty: Wage theft: employer liability plus damages; failure to provide sick time: BOLI enforcement and civil liability
exceptions: Casual domestic employment
Some seasonal agricultural work

laws.title: Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts
laws.subtitle: Nation's Most Expansive School Voucher Program
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) program — expanded to universal eligibility in 2022 — gives every Arizona K-12 student the ability to use approximately $7,000 of state education funding for private school tuition, home school materials, tutoring, or other approved education expenses. Arizona became the first state with a truly universal school voucher program, applicable to all students regardless of income or circumstance. Critics argue the program primarily benefits families already in private school and drains public school funding. The program has cost significantly more than projected.
laws.penalty: ESA funds must be used for approved educational expenses; auditing of spending; misuse results in repayment and eligibility loss
exceptions: Students must be Arizona residents
Spending must be on approved education categories

laws.title: SB 1070: Support Our Law Enforcement Act
laws.subtitle: Arizona's controversial 'show your papers' law
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's SB 1070 (2010) was the strictest state immigration law of its time, requiring police to check immigration status during lawful stops if they had 'reasonable suspicion' of illegal status, making it a state crime to be in Arizona without immigration papers, and prohibiting day laborers from soliciting work from vehicles. The law sparked national boycotts of Arizona. The Supreme Court (Arizona v. United States, 2012) struck down three of four key provisions but upheld the 'show your papers' requirement. The law influenced similar legislation in other states.
laws.penalty: Failure to carry immigration documents is a state misdemeanor under surviving provisions; local governments cannot restrict police from asking about immigration status
exceptions: US citizens do not need to carry immigration papers
Lawful permanent residents carrying their green cards satisfy the documentation requirement
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona SB 1070 (2010) and Arizona v. United States

quiz.q: The Supreme Court struck down most of Arizona's SB 1070 in 2012 but upheld which provision?
options: Making it a state crime to work without authorization
The 'show your papers' requirement allowing police to check immigration status
Prohibiting day laborers from soliciting work
Making it illegal for undocumented immigrants to apply for work
quiz.explanation: In Arizona v. United States (2012), the Supreme Court struck down three provisions of SB 1070 as federal preemption violations, but upheld Section 2(B) — the 'show your papers' requirement allowing police to check immigration status during lawful stops.

laws.title: Proposition 207: Smart and Safe Arizona Act
laws.subtitle: Arizona's cannabis legalization and criminal justice
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Proposition 207 (2020) legalized recreational cannabis for adults 21+ and created the Arizona Department of Health Services cannabis licensing. Arizona allows social consumption in licensed venues (cannabis lounges). Arizona previously had harsh drug laws, including mandatory minimums for drug possession regardless of quantity. Prop 207 required expungement of prior cannabis convictions. Arizona also implemented Proposition 200 (1996) mandating drug treatment (not incarceration) for first and second time drug possession offenders — an early diversion approach.
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession over 1 oz (28.5g): civil penalty; sales without license: felony; methamphetamine possession: felony; Proposition 200 mandates drug treatment diversion for first-time possession offenses
exceptions: Adults 21+ may possess up to 1 oz cannabis (5g concentrate)
Home cultivation of up to 6 plants permitted
Proposition 200 requires treatment not jail for first/second time simple possession of any drug

quiz.q: Arizona's Proposition 200 (1996) was progressive for its time because it required what for first-time drug possession offenders?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Prop 200 mandated drug treatment (not incarceration) for first and second time simple drug possession offenders, making Arizona an early adopter of the treatment-over-incarceration approach to drug policy that has since spread to many other jurisdictions.

laws.title: Arizona LGBTQ+ Rights Landscape
laws.subtitle: Arizona's limited LGBTQ+ protections
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has limited state-level LGBTQ+ protections. Arizona has no statewide non-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations. Same-sex marriage was legalized by federal court order (2014, before Obergefell). Arizona has repeatedly attempted and failed to pass an SB 1062 (2014) religious exemption bill that would have allowed businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ+ individuals (vetoed by Governor Brewer). Local ordinances in Phoenix, Tucson, Tempe, and other cities provide some protections.
laws.penalty: Without state-level LGBTQ+ non-discrimination law, most state-level civil remedies are unavailable; federal protections (Bostock) apply to employment; local ordinance violations are handled at city level with varying penalties
exceptions: Federal employment protections (Bostock v. Clayton County) apply regardless of state law
Local non-discrimination ordinances in major cities provide some protection
Federal Fair Housing Act provides limited sexual orientation protections
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona Attorney General Civil Rights Division

quiz.q: Arizona Governor Jan Brewer vetoed SB 1062 in 2014. What would this law have allowed?
options: Businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ+ individuals based on religious beliefs
Transgender people to use bathrooms matching their identity
quiz.explanation: SB 1062 would have expanded Arizona's Religious Freedom Restoration Act to explicitly allow businesses and individuals to refuse service to LGBTQ+ people based on religious beliefs. Governor Brewer vetoed it after intense national pressure, including from major corporations and the NFL (which threatened to move the Super Bowl).

laws.title: Reporter Privilege and Border Journalism Risks
laws.subtitle: Arizona has shield law protections but journalists face unique risks covering border issues
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's reporter shield law (ARS 12-2237) provides qualified privilege against compelled disclosure of confidential sources. Arizona journalists, particularly those covering the US-Mexico border, immigration enforcement, and drug trafficking, face unique safety and legal risks. The state has a Public Records Law. Arizona journalists have been caught in difficult situations during border enforcement operations. The state's journalism community has advocated for stronger protections. Several journalists have been investigated or threatened while covering sensitive border stories.
laws.penalty: Qualified reporter privilege; can be overcome in criminal proceedings with sufficient showing
exceptions: Criminal proceedings and national security investigations may override the privilege

quiz.q: What unique challenge do Arizona journalists face that journalists in most other US states do not?
options: Covering the US-Mexico border with associated safety and legal risks
quiz.explanation: Arizona journalists, particularly those covering the US-Mexico border, face unique challenges including safety risks from drug trafficking and immigration enforcement operations, cross-border legal complications, and interaction with multiple law enforcement agencies.

laws.title: Social Media Parental Consent Laws
laws.subtitle: Arizona requires parental consent for minors using social media platforms
laws.fullDescription: Arizona passed HB 2132 (2024), requiring social media platforms to obtain parental consent before allowing users under 18 to create accounts. The law also requires platforms to provide parental controls and the ability for parents to monitor and delete their child's account. Arizona's law is part of a nationwide wave of state-level children's online safety legislation. Arizona has also passed data breach notification laws and consumer privacy legislation. The state's proximity to the US-Mexico border creates unique digital privacy considerations around immigration-related data.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties for platforms that allow minors to create accounts without parental consent
exceptions: First Amendment challenges are likely as courts evaluate similar laws

quiz.q: What does Arizona's HB 2132 (2024) require for minors under 18 on social media?
options: Parental consent before account creation plus parental controls
quiz.explanation: Arizona's HB 2132 (2024) requires social media platforms to obtain parental consent before allowing users under 18 to create accounts, and mandates parental monitoring controls and the ability to delete children's accounts — part of a nationwide wave of state children's online safety laws.

laws.title: Arizona's Financial Sandbox and Banking Regulation
laws.subtitle: Arizona's regulatory sandbox allows fintech companies to test innovative financial products
laws.fullDescription: Arizona launched one of the first fintech regulatory sandboxes in the US (2018), allowing innovative financial companies to test products with limited regulatory requirements for up to two years. The Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions (DIFI) oversees banking and financial services. Arizona has a significant credit union sector and community banking presence. Arizona's banking history includes significant failures during the savings and loan crisis. Arizona's border with Mexico makes remittance services and cross-border banking particularly significant.
laws.penalty: DIFI regulatory enforcement; sandbox participants have limited exemptions; violations outside sandbox subject to standard penalties
exceptions: Sandbox participants receive regulatory relief for approved testing periods

quiz.q: What innovative regulatory tool did Arizona launch in 2018 for the financial industry?
options: A fintech regulatory sandbox for testing financial products
quiz.explanation: Arizona launched one of the first fintech regulatory sandboxes in the US in 2018, allowing innovative financial companies to test products with limited regulatory requirements for up to two years — a model later adopted by other US states and countries seeking to attract financial innovation.

laws.title: Arizona Food Code & Farm Stand Exemptions
laws.subtitle: Arizona balances standard food safety with broad agricultural exemptions
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Department of Health Services (ADHS) enforces the Arizona Food Code, based on the FDA model Food Code. Arizona has specific rules for its unique food environment — including regulations for desert-grown foods and agricultural products. Arizona has broad farm stand and agricultural sales exemptions that allow farmers to sell produce directly without the same requirements as commercial food establishments. Arizona also has a cottage food law allowing home producers to sell non-potentially-hazardous foods directly to consumers. Arizona's hot climate requires strict temperature control for food safety. The state has specific rules for food banks and donation of food to nonprofits, encouraging food recovery.
laws.penalty: Food establishment violations: ADHS can issue civil penalties; critical violations: immediate closure orders; food fraud: criminal charges under Arizona Revised Statutes
exceptions: Farm stands selling only products grown on that farm have broad exemptions
Cottage food producers selling directly at farmers markets have simplified licensing
Religious food service for congregation use is generally exempt

quiz.q: What environmental factor makes temperature control particularly critical for food safety in Arizona?
options: Extreme heat accelerating bacterial growth and food spoilage
Low humidity causing rapid food dehydration
quiz.explanation: Arizona's extreme heat — regularly exceeding 110°F (43°C) in summer — dramatically accelerates bacterial growth in improperly stored foods. The temperature danger zone (40°F-140°F) poses significantly elevated risk in Arizona's climate, making cold chain management critical.

laws.title: Arizona Anti-Cruelty Laws and Hot Car Animal Rescue
laws.subtitle: Arizona allows civilians to rescue animals from hot vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Arizona Revised Statutes 13-2910 covers cruelty to animals, making it a class 1 misdemeanor for neglect and class 6 felony for intentional torture or killing. Notably, Arizona's HB 2494 (2016) authorizes private citizens — not just law enforcement — to forcibly enter a vehicle to rescue an animal in imminent danger from heat or cold, provided they notify police first and use minimum necessary force. Arizona also has livestock cruelty laws (ARS 3-2157) and prohibits animal fighting. The state has a 'Pets in Emergency Shelters' law requiring emergency shelters to accept pets during disasters, recognizing the public safety risk of pet owners refusing to evacuate without their animals.
laws.penalty: Class 1 misdemeanor: up to 6 months and $2,500 fine; class 6 felony: up to 2 years; commercial animal fighting: class 5 felony up to 2.5 years
exceptions: Standard agricultural practices
Licensed hunting, trapping, and fishing
Research under USDA oversight
Rodeo events under professional sanctioning

quiz.q: What does Arizona's 2016 HB 2494 authorize regarding animals in hot vehicles?
options: Only police may rescue animals from vehicles
Any person may forcibly enter a vehicle to rescue an animal in imminent danger after notifying police
Animal control must respond within 10 minutes
Vehicles must be towed if animals are inside
quiz.explanation: Arizona's 2016 law uniquely allows any private citizen (not just law enforcement) to forcibly enter a vehicle to rescue an animal facing imminent danger from heat or cold, provided they notify police first and use only necessary force.

laws.title: Arizona Community Property and Joint Custody Presumption
laws.subtitle: Arizona presumes equal parenting time in divorce cases
laws.fullDescription: Arizona is a community property state — all marital property divided equally. Arizona took a significant step in 2013 by enacting a statutory presumption of joint custody ('legal decision-making and parenting time') in divorce cases. Courts must consider why joint custody would not be in the child's best interests before awarding sole custody. Arizona family courts use 'legal decision-making' (major decisions about education, healthcare, religion) and 'parenting time' as the two custody components. Arizona's Covenant Marriage Act (1998) — the first in the US — created a harder-to-dissolve marriage option. Arizona has robust domestic violence protections including Orders of Protection and military family provisions.
laws.penalty: Contempt of court for violating orders; child support non-compliance: licence suspension, wage garnishment, tax refund capture; criminal sanctions possible for repeated violations
exceptions: Premarital agreements valid if voluntarily signed with independent counsel
Separate property not subject to community property rules
Covenant marriage has different divorce requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona Revised Statutes Title 25 — Marital and Domestic Relations

quiz.q: What presumption did Arizona add to its child custody law in 2013?
options: A presumption that mothers receive primary custody
A presumption of joint custody — courts must justify why joint parenting time is not appropriate
A presumption that children choose their custodian at age 10
A presumption against shared custody in different school districts
quiz.explanation: Arizona's 2013 legislative change created a presumption of joint legal decision-making and parenting time — placing the burden on the court to explain why joint custody is NOT appropriate rather than why it should be. This significantly shifted Arizona toward shared parenting as the default outcome.

laws.title: Arizona Landlord Rights & Property Tax Protections
laws.subtitle: Landlord-friendly state with strong property owner rights
laws.fullDescription: Arizona is one of the most landlord-friendly states in the U.S. State law preempts all local rent control (A.R.S. § 33-1329). The Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets a streamlined 5-day notice for nonpayment of rent before eviction proceedings. The state's homestead exemption protects up to $400,000 of home equity from creditors (A.R.S. § 33-1101). Arizona also has strong protections against regulatory takings under Proposition 207 (2006).
laws.penalty: 5-day cure-or-quit for nonpayment; $400,000 homestead exemption from most creditor claims
exceptions: State preempts all local rent control
Fast-track eviction process

quiz.q: How large is Arizona's homestead exemption protecting home equity from creditors?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's homestead exemption (A.R.S. § 33-1101) protects up to $400,000 of equity in a primary residence from most creditor claims, significantly increased from the prior $150,000 limit.

laws.title: Arizona Consumer Fraud Act & Data Privacy Rules
laws.subtitle: Consumer fraud protections and growing data rights
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act (A.R.S. § 44-1521) prohibits deceptive acts in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise. The AG can seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation. Private consumers can recover actual damages but not attorney fees under the state act (though federal laws may provide fee shifting). Arizona enacted a data breach notification law requiring notice within 45 days. The Arizona Lemon Law covers new motor vehicles with defects materially impairing use, safety, or value. Arizona is relatively consumer-law moderate compared to California or New York, with fewer plaintiff-friendly private remedies.
laws.penalty: Consumer Fraud Act: AG civil penalties up to $10,000; data breach violation: up to $10,000 per day
exceptions: Private plaintiffs cannot recover attorney fees under state Consumer Fraud Act
45-day data breach notification window

quiz.q: Under Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act, what key remedy is NOT available to private consumers?
quiz.explanation: Unlike many states, Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act does not provide private consumers with attorney fees recovery — a significant limitation since attorney fees often determine whether a consumer can find a lawyer to take a small-value fraud case.

laws.title: SB 1070 — Arizona's Immigration Law
laws.subtitle: Support Our Law Enforcement and Safe Neighborhoods Act (2010)
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's SB 1070 (2010) required police to check immigration status during lawful stops when there was reasonable suspicion. Much of the law was struck down by the US Supreme Court (Arizona v. United States, 2012), but the 'show me your papers' provision was upheld. The law sparked national debate about state immigration enforcement.
laws.penalty: State penalties mostly preempted by federal law; remaining provisions allow status checks.
exceptions: US Supreme Court struck most provisions as federal preemption
Show-me-your-papers provision (§2B) upheld but must not prolong stops
Federal law controls immigration enforcement
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona SB 1070 & Arizona v. United States

quiz.q: Which provision of Arizona's SB 1070 did the US Supreme Court uphold in 2012?
options: Making it a state crime to be undocumented
The 'show me your papers' check during lawful stops
Prohibiting undocumented workers from seeking employment
quiz.explanation: The US Supreme Court (Arizona v. United States, 2012) struck most of SB 1070 as federal preemption but upheld §2B — the 'show me your papers' provision requiring status checks during lawful stops, while prohibiting prolonged detention.

laws.title: Arizona Groundwater Management Act — AMA System
laws.subtitle: Arizona Groundwater Code (1980) — Nation's strictest
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's 1980 Groundwater Management Act created Active Management Areas (AMAs) around Phoenix, Tucson, Prescott, and other cities. AMAs require permits, impose pumping limits, and mandate a 100-year safe water supply for new subdivisions. Arizona is the only western state with comprehensive groundwater regulation. The 2023 Rio Verde water crisis highlighted ongoing challenges.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized groundwater pumping in AMAs: civil penalties, well closure.
exceptions: Rural areas outside AMAs have less regulation
Agricultural uses in AMAs have grandfathered pumping rights
Mining operations have specific permitting

quiz.q: What must Arizona developers prove before building new subdivisions in Active Management Areas?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Groundwater Management Act requires developers in Active Management Areas (AMAs) to demonstrate a 100-year assured water supply before subdivisions can be approved — a uniquely stringent requirement designed to prevent development outpacing water availability.

laws.title: Arizona Commerce Authority & Business Incentives
laws.subtitle: Arizona Revised Statutes §41-1500 — Economic development
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has aggressively attracted major manufacturers with tax incentives. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) chose Phoenix for a $40 billion chip plant partly due to Arizona Commerce Authority incentives. Arizona offers Quality Jobs Tax Credits, foreign trade zones, and low corporate income tax. Arizona's economy diversified from agriculture to high-tech.
laws.penalty: N/A — incentive program.
exceptions: Incentives subject to job creation and wage commitments
Clawback provisions if commitments not met
Some sectors get enhanced incentives (semiconductor, EV)

quiz.q: Which major semiconductor company chose Phoenix for a $40 billion chip plant?
quiz.explanation: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company) chose Phoenix, Arizona for its North American manufacturing expansion — a $40 billion investment partly attracted by Arizona's business incentives and semiconductor workforce development.

laws.title: School Voucher Program — Education Savings Accounts
laws.subtitle: Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts — Universal ESA
laws.fullDescription: Arizona expanded its Education Savings Account (ESA) program in 2022 to be universal — available to all K-12 students, not just those with disabilities or from failing schools. Parents receive approximately $7,000/year (per-pupil funding minus administrative costs) to spend on private school, tutoring, homeschool materials, or other education expenses. The most expansive program in the US.
laws.penalty: Misuse of ESA funds: repayment, disqualification from future participation.
exceptions: Public school students may use ESA only if they leave public school
Funds may not be used for religious instruction costs separately — but private religious schools are eligible
Annual renewal required
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona Dept. of Education ESA Program

quiz.q: Who is eligible for Arizona's universal Education Savings Account (ESA) program?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's 2022 ESA expansion made it universal — any K-12 student in Arizona can receive state ESA funds (approximately $7,000/year) for private school, homeschool, or tutoring, regardless of income or special needs.

laws.title: Arizona Proposition 209 — Medical Debt Protection (2022)
laws.subtitle: Homestead protection & medical debt reform
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters approved Prop 209 in 2022, dramatically strengthening protections against medical debt collection. Homestead exemption increased from $250,000 to $400,000. Wage garnishment protection increased (health care debts limited to 10% of disposable income). Maximum interest on medical debt capped at 3%. One of the strongest medical debt protections in the US.
laws.penalty: N/A — this restricts debt collection.
exceptions: Voluntary payment plans outside these protections
Federal tax liens not affected
Child support and alimony enforcement unaffected

quiz.q: What did Arizona Proposition 209 (2022) limit the interest rate on medical debt to?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Proposition 209 capped interest on medical debt at 3% — dramatically below the prior maximum. Combined with increased wage garnishment protections, it is one of the nation's strongest medical debt shields.

laws.title: Constitutional Carry — No Permit for Open or Concealed Carry
laws.subtitle: Arizona Revised Statutes §13-3102 — Permitless carry since 2010
laws.fullDescription: Arizona was among the first states to allow permitless carry of firearms (2010). Adults 21+ (18+ for open carry) who are legally allowed to possess firearms may carry openly or concealed without a permit. Arizona Concealed Weapons Permits are still available for those wanting reciprocity in other states. Arizona has very few firearm restrictions.
laws.penalty: Carrying while prohibited (felons, domestic abusers): class 4 felony.
exceptions: Federal gun-free zones (schools, federal buildings) still apply
Bars and restaurants may prohibit carry
Cannot carry if under 21 for concealed (18+ for open carry)

quiz.q: What is the minimum age for permitted concealed carry in Arizona?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's permitless concealed carry requires being at least 21 years old. Open carry (without permit) is legal for adults 18 and older. Anyone legally prohibited from possessing firearms may not carry.

laws.title: Solar Energy Capital — Net Metering & Solar Rights
laws.subtitle: Arizona solar regulations — Abundant sunshine
laws.fullDescription: Arizona receives more sun than almost any US state. Arizona has a 'solar rights' law preventing HOAs from banning rooftop solar. Net metering (selling excess solar to the grid) is regulated by the ACC (Arizona Corporation Commission). In 2017, APS (Arizona Public Service) won a rate change reducing net metering rates. Arizona has nation-leading utility-scale solar.
laws.penalty: HOAs that ban rooftop solar: unenforceable restrictions, potential lawsuits.
exceptions: Reasonable aesthetic restrictions by HOAs still allowed
Historic districts may restrict solar panel placement
Net metering rates subject to ACC determination

quiz.q: Can Arizona HOAs prohibit homeowners from installing rooftop solar panels?
options: No, Arizona's solar rights law prevents outright bans
Only if the solar panels face the street
Only for homes under certain value
quiz.explanation: Arizona's solar rights law prohibits HOAs from completely banning rooftop solar installations. HOAs may impose reasonable aesthetic restrictions (size, placement, appearance) but cannot outright prohibit solar.

laws.title: Automated Traffic Enforcement — Speed Cameras
laws.subtitle: Arizona statutes on photo enforcement — Limited use
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has a complicated history with speed cameras. After a statewide program was ended in 2010 due to public opposition (and a camera operator was shot), use moved to local option. Phoenix, Scottsdale, and some freeways use cameras. Arizona law limits school zone camera use. Photo enforcement fines require actual service of citation.
laws.penalty: Photo enforcement fines: typically $181 for highway violations. Unserved citations can be dismissed.
exceptions: Citations must be personally served or mailed within required time
Some citations can be avoided if not personally served
Constitutional challenge allowed in court

quiz.q: What happened to Arizona's statewide highway speed camera program in 2010?
options: It was ended after public opposition
It was sold to a private company
It was moved to local government control only
quiz.explanation: Arizona's statewide highway speed camera program was terminated in 2010 following significant public opposition. An incident where a camera van operator was shot also contributed to the program's end.

laws.title: Medical Marijuana — Prop 203 (2010)
laws.subtitle: Arizona Medical Marijuana Act — 25% of vote passed it
laws.fullDescription: Arizona legalized medical marijuana by the narrowest possible margin (50.13%) in 2010. Recreational use was legalized in 2020 (Prop 207, 60%). Arizona's Medical Marijuana Act allows patients with qualifying conditions to purchase up to 2.5 oz per 2-week period from dispensaries. Arizona had early dispensary rollout challenges due to narrow passage.
laws.penalty: Recreational possession over 1 oz: class 6 felony. Illegal sale: class 3 felony.
exceptions: Medical patients may possess more under certain circumstances
Home cultivation: 6 plants for medical patients in areas over 25 miles from dispensary
Adults 21+ may possess 1 oz and grow 6 plants under Prop 207

quiz.q: By what margin did Arizona voters pass medical marijuana in 2010?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Prop 203 (medical marijuana, 2010) passed by just 50.13% — one of the closest margins for any medical cannabis initiative in US history. Recreational cannabis (Prop 207) passed more comfortably at 60% in 2020.

laws.title: Proposition 300 — Tuition for Undocumented Students
laws.subtitle: Arizona Prop 300 (2006) — No in-state tuition without status
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters approved Prop 300 in 2006, prohibiting undocumented immigrants from receiving in-state tuition or most state financial aid. This directly conflicted with DACA recipients seeking in-state tuition. A 2019 Arizona court ruling found DACA recipients may qualify for in-state tuition. Arizona's laws around undocumented immigrants are among the nation's strictest.
laws.penalty: Institutions improperly granting in-state tuition: loss of state funding.
exceptions: DACA recipients may qualify per court rulings
Legally present immigrants qualify
Federal financial aid (Pell grants) not affected by state rules

quiz.q: What did Arizona's Proposition 300 (2006) prohibit for undocumented immigrants?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Proposition 300 prohibited undocumented immigrants from receiving in-state tuition rates at public universities and most forms of state financial aid. Later court rulings created exceptions for DACA recipients.

laws.title: Sonoran Desert Saguaro Cactus Protection
laws.subtitle: Arizona Native Plant Law — Protected saguaros
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's Native Plant Law protects saguaro cacti and other native plants. Moving or destroying a saguaro requires a permit (Saguaro Cactus Permit). Native plants on state, federal, or private land cannot be removed without permits. Saguaros can live 150-200 years. Bootlegging cacti (illegally removing and selling them) is a serious crime.
laws.penalty: Destroying or removing saguaro without permit: class 4 felony (up to $150,000 fine, 3.75 years prison).
exceptions: Permitted construction projects can relocate saguaros with prior approval
Property owners can get permits for safety removals
Commercial nurseries may have permits for legally acquired plants
laws.sourceLabel: Arizona Dept. of Agriculture — Native Plants

quiz.q: What is the penalty for illegally removing or destroying a saguaro cactus in Arizona?
options: Class 4 felony (up to $150,000 and prison time)
quiz.explanation: Illegally removing or destroying a saguaro cactus in Arizona is a class 4 felony, potentially resulting in up to $150,000 in fines and 3.75 years in prison. The saguaro is an iconic Arizona symbol given extensive legal protection.

laws.title: Independent Redistricting Commission
laws.subtitle: Arizona Prop 106 (2000) — Citizens draw legislative maps
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters created an Independent Redistricting Commission in 2000 to draw congressional and legislative district lines, removing the process from the legislature. The 5-member commission (2 Republicans, 2 Democrats, 1 independent) draws maps with transparency. The Arizona Supreme Court upheld it; it survived a US Supreme Court challenge (Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona IRC, 2015).
laws.penalty: Legislative interference with IRC: potential constitutional violation.
exceptions: Commission itself is not immune from lawsuits challenging maps
VRA compliance required
Commission decisions subject to judicial review

quiz.q: How many members serve on Arizona's Independent Redistricting Commission?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Independent Redistricting Commission has 5 members: 2 Republicans, 2 Democrats, and 1 independent (selected from a pool by the Commission on Appellate Court Appointments). The commission was upheld by the US Supreme Court in 2015.

laws.title: FinTech Regulatory Sandbox
laws.subtitle: Arizona FinTech Sandbox — Innovation-friendly regulation
laws.fullDescription: Arizona launched the nation's first Financial Technology Regulatory Sandbox in 2018, allowing FinTech companies to test innovative financial products with up to 10,000 customers without full regulatory compliance. The sandbox provides 2 years (extendable to 3) of regulatory relief while companies prove their model. Arizona AG oversees the program.
laws.penalty: Fraud or consumer harm within sandbox: immediate removal, full enforcement.
exceptions: Participants limited to 10,000 Arizona customers during sandbox
Must apply and be accepted
Cannot offer products in other states under sandbox protection

quiz.q: Arizona launched the nation's first of what type of regulatory program in 2018?
quiz.explanation: Arizona launched the nation's first Financial Technology Regulatory Sandbox in 2018, allowing FinTech companies to test innovative products with limited customers without full regulatory compliance — a model adopted by other states and countries.

laws.title: No Front License Plate Required
laws.subtitle: Arizona ADOT — Single plate state
laws.fullDescription: Arizona is one of about 19 US states that only requires a rear license plate — no front plate needed. This means vehicle owners don't need to drill into their front bumpers. Some vehicles (specialty, vintage) may have additional exemptions. Arizona's plate comes in multiple designs including the iconic Saguaro cactus design.
laws.penalty: Rear plate violations: $135+ fine. Non-compliant specialty plates: $25–$50.
exceptions: Temporary permits when plate pending
Dealer plates during test drives
Historic vehicles have separate plate rules

quiz.q: How many license plates does Arizona require on registered vehicles?
quiz.explanation: Arizona only requires one license plate — on the rear of the vehicle. This is a convenience that means owners of new vehicles don't need to modify their front bumpers to mount a plate.

laws.title: Extreme Heat Laws — Exposure of Vulnerable Persons
laws.subtitle: Arizona Revised Statutes §13-3623 — Endangerment in heat
laws.fullDescription: Arizona regularly hits 110°F+ in Phoenix. Arizona law criminalizes leaving vulnerable persons (children, elderly, pets) in hot vehicles or extreme heat exposure conditions. 'Vulnerable adult' abuse includes heat exposure neglect. During monsoon season and extreme heat, emergency orders may trigger additional protections. The Sonoran Desert heat is uniquely deadly.
laws.penalty: Leaving child in hot vehicle (death): up to murder charges. Vulnerable adult abuse: class 4 felony.
exceptions: Emergency situations — medical crisis requiring vehicle exit
Law enforcement may break windows to rescue those in danger (protected from liability)
Good Samaritan law protects rescuers

quiz.q: At what temperature can the interior of a car in Arizona sun reach, making heat exposure deadly?
quiz.explanation: On a 100°F Arizona day, a car's interior can exceed 160°F within minutes — temperatures that cause rapid heat stroke and death. This is why Arizona law criminalizes leaving children or vulnerable adults in parked vehicles.

laws.title: Clean Elections Act — Public Campaign Financing
laws.subtitle: Arizona Prop 200 (1998) — State-funded campaign option
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters created a Clean Elections system in 1998, allowing candidates for state office to opt for public financing. Candidates who qualify (by collecting small $5 contributions from registered voters) receive public funds for their campaigns. In 2011, the US Supreme Court struck down the matching funds provision, reducing the program's impact.
laws.penalty: Clean Elections violations: fines, repayment, disqualification.
exceptions: Federal candidates not covered
Participating candidates must forgo private fundraising
Contribution violations subject to Arizona Citizens Clean Elections Commission enforcement

quiz.q: What must Clean Elections candidates do to qualify for public campaign funding in Arizona?
options: Collect a minimum number of $5 contributions from registered voters
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Clean Elections candidates qualify for public funding by collecting a required number of $5 qualifying contributions from registered voters in their district, demonstrating community support.

laws.title: Border Wall & State-Federal Tensions
laws.subtitle: Arizona-Mexico border — State enforcement actions
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has frequently clashed with the federal government over border enforcement. Governor Ducey installed state-funded shipping containers as a border wall barrier in 2022. Governor Hobbs ordered their removal in 2023. Arizona has deployed National Guard troops under Operation Secure Our Border. The state-federal conflict over immigration enforcement is ongoing.
laws.penalty: Trespassing into the US from Mexico: federal misdemeanor (first offense), federal felony (subsequent).
exceptions: Legal ports of entry for authorized crossings
Asylum seekers may present at ports of entry
Humanitarian aid organizations have legal protection for water/food near border

quiz.q: What improvised border barrier did Arizona Governor Ducey install in 2022?
quiz.explanation: Arizona Governor Ducey ordered shipping containers to be stacked along gaps in the US-Mexico border fence in 2022 using state funds. Governor Hobbs ordered their removal in 2023 after taking office.

laws.title: Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC) — Utility Regulation
laws.subtitle: Elected utility regulator — Unique constitutional status
laws.fullDescription: Arizona's ACC is a unique constitutional body — an elected commission that regulates public utilities (electric, gas, telephone, water). Unlike most states where utility regulators are appointed, Arizona voters directly elect the 5 ACC commissioners. The ACC approves utility rate increases, renewable energy standards, and net metering rules. Utilities cannot increase rates without ACC approval.
laws.penalty: Utilities operating without ACC approval: fines, service orders.
exceptions: Federal power lines crossing state may have different regulation
Municipal utilities may be self-regulated
Federal agencies not subject to ACC jurisdiction

quiz.q: How are Arizona Corporation Commission members who regulate utilities selected?
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Corporation Commission (ACC) — which regulates electric, gas, water, and telephone utilities — is unique because its 5 members are directly elected by Arizona voters, not appointed. This gives voters direct control over utility oversight.

laws.title: Arizona Prop 209 — Affirmative Action Ban
laws.subtitle: Prop 107 (2010) — No race in state decisions
laws.fullDescription: Arizona voters banned affirmative action in state employment, education, and contracting in 2010 (Prop 107), joining California, Michigan, Washington, and others. Public universities cannot consider race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in admissions. This preceded the 2023 US Supreme Court ruling (SFFA v. Harvard/UNC) which extended the ban nationally.
laws.penalty: State agencies using race in decisions: civil liability, AG enforcement.
exceptions: Private universities not covered by state ban
Federal contractors may still need to meet federal affirmative action requirements
Outreach and recruitment programs to diverse communities may continue

quiz.q: What did Arizona's Proposition 107 (2010) ban in state government decisions?
options: Using race or sex as a factor in state employment, education, or contracting
quiz.explanation: Arizona's Prop 107 (2010) amended the state constitution to prohibit state agencies, universities, and contractors from considering race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in their decisions — banning affirmative action.

laws.title: Abortion — Near-Total Ban & Constitutional Protection Battle
laws.subtitle: Arizona abortion law — Ongoing legal conflict post-Dobbs
laws.fullDescription: Arizona has had conflicting abortion laws. After Dobbs (2022), a Civil War-era (1864) near-total abortion ban was initially reinstated by courts, then blocked. Arizona voters approved Prop 139 in November 2024 adding abortion rights to the state constitution until 'fetal viability' (about 22-24 weeks). Arizona is now a constitutional protection state for abortion access.
laws.penalty: Abortion providers in violation of state law: license revocation, criminal charges.
exceptions: Prop 139 (2024) protects abortion until fetal viability
Medical emergency exceptions apply
Licensed physicians required for all procedures

quiz.q: What did Arizona voters approve in November 2024 regarding abortion?
options: Abortion rights enshrined in the state constitution until fetal viability
quiz.explanation: Arizona voters approved Proposition 139 in November 2024, amending the state constitution to protect abortion access until fetal viability (approximately 22-24 weeks), overriding the previously contested 1864 near-total ban.
